prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff passenger.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that the Montreal Convention's two-year limitations period is a condition precedent to suit that may nonetheless be affected by equitable considerations, or alternatively the airline's bankruptcy stay tolls it.

Cite at least six decisions of the Eleventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
# ARGUMENT

## I. Article 35's Two-Year Period Is a Condition Precedent, but It Does Not Foreclose Equitable Relief in Extraordinary Circumstances.

Article 35(1) of the Montreal Convention provides that "[t]he right to damages shall be extinguished if an action is not brought within a period of two years." Article 35(2) adds that "[t]he method of calculating that period shall be determined by the law of the court seised of the case." Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules for International Carriage by Air arts. 35(1)–(2), May 28, 1999, S. Treaty Doc. No. 106-45, 2242 U.N.T.S. 309. Plaintiff does not dispute that timely suit is a condition of the right to recover. *See Fishman v. Delta Air Lines, Inc.*, 132 F.3d 138, 142–43 (2d Cir. 1998) (Warsaw Convention). But the label does not resolve whether forum law may adjust how the period is computed.

Article 35(2) expressly delegates the "method of calculating" the period to the law of the forum. In this Circuit, that law includes equitable tolling, which the Court has long applied to statutory periods that bar a claim if missed. *See Justice v. United States*, 6 F.3d 1474, 1479 (11th Cir. 1993) (Federal Tort Claims Act); *Cabello v. Fernandez-Larios*, 402 F.3d 1148, 1154–55 (11th Cir. 2005) (Torture Victim Protection Act and Alien Tort Statute); *Arce v. Garcia*, 434 F.3d 1254, 1261–65 (11th Cir. 2006) (same); *Drew v. Dep't of Corr.*, 297 F.3d 1278, 1286–87 (11th Cir. 2002) (AEDPA); *Steed v. Head*, 219 F.3d 1298, 1300 (11th Cir. 2000) (same). Tolling is warranted when a plaintiff's untimeliness results from "extraordinary circumstances that are both beyond [her] control and unavoidable even with diligence." *Sandvik v. United States*, 177 F.3d 1269, 1271 (11th Cir. 1999). Plaintiff acknowledges that this is an "extraordinary remedy" to be "applied sparingly." *Bost v. Fed. Express Corp.*, 372 F.3d 1233, 1242 (11th Cir. 2004). Reading Article 35(2) to incorporate that settled body of forum law gives effect to both paragraphs of Article 35. It does not displace the condition in paragraph (1). It simply honors the Convention's instruction on how the period is calculated.

Plaintiff recognizes that the Ninth Circuit has held that Article 35 bars tolling altogether. *Narayanan v. British Airways*, 747 F.3d 1125, 1128–29 (9th Cir. 2014). That decision does not bind this Court, and this Court has not adopted it. It also gives no independent meaning to Article 35(2), because it treats "extinguished" as if the delegation to forum law did not exist. Because the Convention's text expressly looks to forum law, and the forum's law recognizes tolling for diligent plaintiffs, this Court should hold that equitable considerations may affect the period.

Here, Plaintiff acted diligently. [Insert facts: date of arrival; date of the airline's petition; steps taken to preserve the claim; date suit was filed.] The airline's bankruptcy was an event beyond Plaintiff's control, and it barred Plaintiff from pursuing the claim in the ordinary course. Those are the circumstances in which *Sandvik* calls for tolling.

## II. Alternatively, the Airline's Bankruptcy Stay Tolled the Period.

Even if Article 35 admits no *equitable* tolling, the Bankruptcy Code supplies tolling by statute. Upon the airline's petition, 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(1) automatically stayed "the commencement or continuation" of any action against the debtor that was or could have been commenced before the petition. The stay is broad and self-executing. *See In re Jove Eng'g, Inc.*, 92 F.3d 1539, 1546 (11th Cir. 1996). Plaintiff could not lawfully have filed against the airline during the stay.

Congress anticipated the resulting limitations problem. Section 108(c) provides that if "applicable nonbankruptcy law" fixes a period for commencing or continuing a civil action against the debtor, and that period has not expired before the petition is filed, the period does not expire until the later of its original end date or thirty days after notice of the stay's termination. 11 U.S.C. § 108(c)(1)–(2). Article 35, which is binding federal treaty law applied in a United States court, is "applicable nonbankruptcy law" within the plain meaning of that provision. Section 108(c) operates by statute rather than by equity, so it requires no showing of extraordinary circumstances and does not depend on whether Article 35 is characterized as a condition precedent. Because Article 35(2) directs the court to apply forum law in calculating the period, § 108(c) governs here.

Plaintiff's [date] filing fell within the extended period. [Insert dates.] The action is therefore timely, and the judgment below should be reversed.
